fields.headline:
1.4
Isotopes
fields.subhead: Count protons, neutrons, and electrons in any isotope, and explain why the neutron count does not change the element.

imageSubjects.section: a graphite crucible and tongs on a dark bench, lit from the left

fields.headline: Two Atoms, Different Masses
fields.subhead: You already know the atomic number identifies the element. Now the neutron count is allowed to change and the atomic number is not.
fields.keyq: If two atoms of carbon have different masses, are they still the same element?

imageSubjects.concept: two identical laboratory balances side by side, one pan slightly lower

fields.headline: Three Words You Need First
fields.subhead: Write these before we go further. Everything after this slide uses them.
fields.k1_b: Atoms of one element with different neutron counts.
fields.k2_b: Protons plus neutrons. Not the mass on the periodic table.
fields.k3_b: How common one isotope is on Earth, as a percent.
fields.mustwrite: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.

imageSubjects.aside: a worn chemistry notebook open to a hand-ruled page

fields.headline: Same Element, Different Mass
fields.subhead: Two atoms of carbon can have different masses. They are still both carbon.
fields.c1_b:
Protons.
Every carbon atom has 6.

Change that and it is not carbon.
fields.c2_b:
Neutrons.
Carbon can have 6, 7, or 8.

The mass changes. The element does not.
fields.mustwrite: The atomic number identifies the element. The mass number does not.

imageSubjects.concept: a block of graphite and a diamond specimen on dark slate

fields.headline: The Three Isotopes of Hydrogen
fields.subhead: One proton in all three. The neutron count does the rest.
fields.k1_b:
1 proton, 0 neutrons
Mass number 1

About 99.98% of all hydrogen.
fields.k2_b:
1 proton, 1 neutron
Mass number 2

Called deuterium.
fields.k3_b:
1 proton, 2 neutrons
Mass number 3

Called tritium. Radioactive.
fields.mustwrite: Isotopes of an element differ only in neutron count.

imageSubjects.aside: three sealed glass ampoules of colourless gas in a row

fields.headline: Two Ways to Write the Same Isotope
fields.subhead: You will see both. They carry exactly the same information.
fields.a2_b: Mass number above, atomic number below.

fields.headline: Getting Neutrons Out of the Notation
fields.subhead: Four steps, and you use the same four every time.
fields.s1_b: Atomic number, off the periodic table.

imageSubjects.band: a periodic table wall chart photographed at a shallow angle

fields.headline: Example: Counting Particles in Chlorine-37
fields.subhead: We do this one together. Copy the setup, not just the answer.
fields.problem: How many protons, neutrons, and electrons are in a neutral atom of chlorine-37?
fields.mustwrite: Neutrons = mass number minus atomic number.

imageSubjects.aside: a bottle of sodium chloride crystals under warm light

fields.headline: Chlorine-37, Worked
fields.subhead: Write the subtraction down. If you do it in your head you will lose track of it on the test.
fields.mustwrite: A neutral atom has equal protons and electrons.

imageSubjects.data: an analytical balance display in a darkened lab

fields.headline: Not All Isotopes Are Equally Common
fields.subhead: Isotopes of an element occur in fixed proportions. Those proportions are measured, not chosen.
fields.c1_b:
About 76% of all chlorine on Earth.

18 neutrons.
fields.mustwrite: Natural abundance is measured in a lab, not decided.

imageSubjects.concept: rock salt crystals spilled across a dark surface

fields.headline: Your Turn: Potassium-40
fields.subhead: Same four steps. Work it in your notes, then we compare.
fields.problem: How many protons, neutrons, and electrons are in a neutral atom of potassium-40?
fields.g1_b:
Potassium-40
Use the periodic table for the atomic number.
fields.mustwrite: Protons plus neutrons must give you back the mass number. Check it every time.

imageSubjects.aside: a potassium chloride reagent bottle with a worn label

fields.headline: Potassium-40, Worked
fields.subhead: Check yours against this before we move on.

imageSubjects.data: a scientist's pencil resting on a page of handwritten calculations
